extracted.intended_audience: patentees, patent agents and legal counsel dealing with Canadian patents (CIPO practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on Canadian Patent Office procedures and substantive criteria for: maintenance fees and deemed expiry, requests to reverse deemed expiry (due care standard and required evidence), corrections to granted patents (obvious errors, naming, specification/drawings), disclaimers, and re-examination proceedings. Focused on administrative requirements and evaluative standards used by the Commissioner and re-examination board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deemed expiry of patents and additional term
rubrics_metrics.description: If the maintenance fee and the late fee are not paid within the late fee period, the term of the patent will be deemed to have expired retroactively at the original maintenance fee due date under subsection 46(4) of the Patent Act and section 113 of the Patent Rules. If the maintenance fee and the late fee are not paid within the late fee period for a patent for which additional term is granted, the additional term of the patent will be deemed to have expired retroactively at the original maintenance fee due date under subsection 46.2(4) of the Patent Act and section 117.06 of the Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies retroactive effect to original due date; applies equally to additional term. The 'late fee period' defined elsewhere (later of six months from due date or two months from notice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy letters of deemed expiry
rubrics_metrics.description: While not required by the Patent Act or the Patent Rules, the Patent Office will endeavour to inform patentees of deemed expiry through a courtesy letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees should note that they will have already received a notice of the potential for deemed expiry if they failed to comply with fee requirements; courtesy letters are not a legal requirement or substitute for statutory deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of deemed expiry — statutory basis
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent or an additional term is deemed to have expired under subsection 46(4) or 46.2(4) of the Patent Act, it is possible, under subsection 46(5) or 46.2(5), to make a request to the Commissioner to reverse the deemed expiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal is contingent on the Commissioner determining that the failure occurred 'in spite of the due care required by the circumstances' (paragraph 46(5)(b) or 46.2(5)(b)). Relevant Patent Rules (sections 116, 117, 117.09, 117.1) set procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for requesting reversal of deemed expiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Under sections 116 and 117.09(1) of the Patent Rules, the time limit for a patentee to request the reversal of a deemed expiry of a patent or of an additional term is 12 months after the end of six months after the applicable maintenance fee due date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the six-month and the 12-month periods are extended under section 78 of the Patent Act if they expire on a prescribed or designated day. Example provided: maintenance due March 31, deemed expired Sept 30; period to request reversal ends on Sept 30 of the next year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due care requirement for reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments implementing the Patent Law Treaty introduce a due care standard that must be met by a patentee who wishes to apply for reversal of deemed expiry because of a failure to pay a maintenance fee and the late fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioner must determine that the failure occurred despite the due care required by the circumstances before deeming the patent never to have expired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional provisions for pre-2019 maintenance dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 78.55 of the Patent Act specifies that section 46, as it read immediately before October 30, 2019, applies to maintenance fee due dates (not including the period of grace) before October 30, 2019.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If maintenance fee due date (excluding period of grace) is before Oct 30, 2019 and fee not paid by that date, the patentee will have a 12-month grace period (see CIPO Patent Fees page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's obligation in Commissioner determination
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for the Commissioner to make a determination, the patentee is required to provide the reasons for the failure to take the action that should have been taken to avoid the deemed expiry of the patent or the additional term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal only follows if applicable statutory requirements are met and the Commissioner informs the patentee of the determination. Patentee must actively submit reasons; passive silence will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due care assessment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether the failure occurred in spite of the required due care, the Commissioner will assess whether the patentee took all measures that a reasonably prudent patent holder would have taken given the set of circumstances related to the failure; measures taken after the failure occurred will not be taken into consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard aligns with approach used for restoration of priority under PCT. Assessment is fact-specific; the Commissioner considers customary diligence a prudent party would exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents for reversal request
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must, within twelve months after the end of six months after the applicable maintenance fee due date, meet the requirements set out in paragraph 46(5)(a) or 46.2(5)(a): make a request for reversal to the Commissioner; state the reasons for the failure to pay the prescribed fee and late fee before the later of 6 months or 2 months from notice; and pay the maintenance fee, pay the late fee and the additional prescribed fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment of fees is required and is part of the statutory requisites; failure to include required elements risks rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended supporting information for reversal requests
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office recommends that the patentee include: the circumstances that led to the failure; the measures the patentee took to avoid the failure (including remedial or alternative steps); and any other justifications. The patentee may also include evidence such as a medical note or affidavits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including documentary evidence assists the Commissioner in assessing due care. Note on privacy references Chapter 8 guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office procedure — determination (considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner will review the reasons to determine whether the failure occurred in spite of due care. The Commissioner will consider whether anything else could have been reasonably expected to have been done to avoid the failure, taking into account the particular circumstances. Measures taken after the failure are disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will have regard to International Bureau/Receiving Office Guidelines (paragraph 166M) but decisions are fact-specific. Emphasis on what a 'reasonably prudent person' would have done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of circumstances favouring a due care determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances where the Commissioner may find that due care was taken include: force majeure (external, unforeseeable/unavoidable events); unexpected illness of patentee/authorized person; facsimile or software submission failure due to external technical problem where alternatives were exhausted; docketing system error; isolated human error by an assistant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples are illustrative and not exhaustive. The applicant must demonstrate they exercised reasonable care under the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of circumstances disfavouring a due care determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances that may favour a determination that due care was not taken include: lack of financing claimed by patentee; human error due to increased workload, lost file, poor organization; lack of knowledge of the Patent Act/Rules; absence from the office because deadline fell on planned vacation or medical appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine organizational mistakes, financial inability, or ignorance of the law are less likely to meet the due care standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to make observations before determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Before any determination that required due care was not taken, the Patent Office will send a letter to the patentee informing them of the Commissioner’s intended determination and provide the patentee with the opportunity to make observations before the end of one month after the date of the letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural right to comment on the intended adverse finding; timelines are strict (one month).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service standard for response to reversal requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the patentee is informed that the Commissioner intends to determine that due care was not taken, they can expect a response to a request for reversal, including the Commissioner’s determination with respect to the due care standard, within two months of receipt of the request in the Office, or two months from receipt of the last correspondence relating to the request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service standard sets expectations for processing times; exceptions exist if patentee is notified of intended adverse finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections to granted patents — overview
rubrics_metrics.description: From time to time, a patent can contain errors due to oversight by the patentee or the Patent Office. Certain errors in granted patents may be corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees are encouraged to review documents prior to submission and review grant copy upon receipt; correction windows are limited and vary by error type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner correction of obvious errors (Commissioner's errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner may under subsection 107(1) of the Patent Rules correct errors made by the Commissioner in the patent or in the specification or drawings referenced in the patent within 12 months after the issue of the patent or on request of the patentee made within that period. To make the correction, it must be obvious from documents on file that something else was intended and that nothing else could have been intended. No fee is required for correction of obvious errors made by the Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office has quality controls but patentees should report errors immediately due to the short correction period. Corrections are limited to obvious mistakes and supported by office file documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and formal requirements for correction requests
rubrics_metrics.description: All requests for corrections of Commissioner’s errors in a granted patent must comply with requirements for submitting written communications (Chapter 2). Every request must include: the patent number; name of the patentee(s); a clear request for correction of an error and any additional information that may be needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If missing required information or fee, Commissioner will send a notice requiring submission within three months; failure to supply renders the request never made. The grant copy should never be submitted. A prescribed fee is required (see Patent Fees) and is not contingent on acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-examination board correction of obvious errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 108 of the Patent Rules, the Commissioner may, on his or her own initiative within six months after the day on which a certificate is issued under section 48.4 of the Patent Act, or on request of the patentee within that period, correct an error by the re-examination board in the certificate if, from documents in the Patent Office possession on that day, it is obvious that something other than what is in the certificate was intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fee to correct this error; no time extension; if accepted, correction considered made on the date the certificate was issued; Commissioner must issue a certificate setting out the correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of naming errors (patentee or inventor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees are able, within 12 months of the patent’s issuance, to request correction of errors in the naming of the patentee or the inventor so long as it does not change their identity under paragraph 109(1)(a) of the Patent Rules. The request must contain a statement that the correction does not add or delete a name or change the identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections that would change identity are not permitted under this provision. Timing: within 12 months of issuance, or before end of 12 months after issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of obvious errors in specification or drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees can, within 12 months of issuance, request correction of obvious errors in the specification or drawings under paragraph 109(1)(b) of the Patent Rules. The error must have been obvious to a person skilled in the art that something else was intended than what appears AND that nothing else could have been intended other than the correction proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High standard: must be obvious to skilled person and unambiguous as to intended text/figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents and procedural rules for error correction requests
rubrics_metrics.description: In accordance with subsection 109(2) of the Patent Rules, the request for correction must contain: an indication that a correction is requested; the patent number; the correction to be made; new pages to replace altered pages, if required; and payment of the prescribed fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If request incomplete or fee unpaid, Commissioner will require patentee to supply missing info/fee within three months or the request is treated as never made. Grant copy should not be submitted. Payment of fee is required regardless of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of corrections in a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Commissioner corrects an error under sections 107, 108 or 109 of the Patent Rules, the Commissioner will issue a certificate setting out the correction. The correction has a retroactive effect and will be considered to have been made on the date on which the patent or certificate was issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections are retroactive to issuance date; certificates document the change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer purpose and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclaimer is a mechanism whereby a patentee may, at any time during the life of a patent, amend a patent to claim less than that which was claimed in the original patent (subsection 48(1) of the Patent Act). It is used where the patentee has, by mistake/accident/inadvertence and without wilful intent to defraud, made a specification 'too broad'. A disclaimer is a renunciation of subject-matter and a clear and unequivocal statement that the original patent claims are too broad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer need not be limited to whole claims; part of a claim may be disclaimed provided the disclaimer does not extend the scope of that or dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements for filing a disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: To file a disclaimer, Form 2 of Schedule 1 of the Patent Rules must be completed and filed with the Patent Office along with the appropriate fee (subsection 48(2) of the Patent Act and section 120 of the Patent Rules). In completing Form 2, the patentee must follow the precise form of subsections 3(1) and 3(2) specifying the subject-matter disclaimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specific wording in Form 2 must be followed; language in Form 2 cannot be used to reformulate or redefine the invention disclosed and claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles of Patent Office and Courts regarding disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing of a disclaimer does not involve examination of the subject-matter by the Patent Office. The Office only ensures the disclaimer is filed in the prescribed form and manner and that the fee is paid. The Commissioner has no discretion to refuse to record it if proper. The onus is on the patentee to show the disclaimer satisfies subsection 48(1) of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity depends on: patentee's state of mind at time of specification preparation; good faith; timeliness; whether disclaimer broadens scope; whether it recasts invention or adds new combination. If courts find disclaimer invalid, disclaimed claims revert, but pre-disclaimer claims may be invalid for overbroad admission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of a disclaimer on proceedings and claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclaimers do not normally affect any court action pending at the time they are made (subsection 48(4)). Following a disclaimer, the remaining claims are deemed to be valid for the matter not disclaimed. The disclaimer is unconditional; the existing claims of the patent are the claims as amended by virtue of the disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A timely valid disclaimer can save an otherwise overbroad claim from finding of invalidity, but it is a renunciation of subject-matter and final in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and scope of re-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of re-examination is to provide a relatively summary and inexpensive alternative to impeachment by litigation, or an opportunity for a patentee to have the Patent Office reconsider the claims of an issued patent. Re-examination is limited to issues arising from the prior art supplied by the requesting party and is generally less comprehensive than a court action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-examination is administrative and generally ex parte; the board cannot test credibility via cross-examination; determinations reviewed by courts on a reasonableness standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a re-examination request
rubrics_metrics.description: A written request must be filed with the appropriate fee and, if requester is a small entity, a small entity declaration. The request must be based on prior art consisting of patents, applications open to public inspection, or printed publications (subsection 48.1(1)). The request must set forth the pertinence of the prior art and the manner of applying it to the claim(s) (subsection 48.1(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At minimum, an acceptable request should articulate the relationship between features of the prior art and features of the claims. The grant copy of a patent should never be submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment and composition of the re-examination board
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt of an acceptable request, the Commissioner establishes a re-examination board. The board must consist of not fewer than three persons, at least two of whom must be Patent Office employees. Board members must not have participated in or advised in the examination of the application from which the patent issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically composed of a Patent Appeal Board member as chair and two patent examiners from the relevant examination division. Commissioner informs patentee of the board composition and then takes no further part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of non-compliant re-examination requests
rubrics_metrics.description: If a request does not satisfy subsections 48.1(1) or (2) or section 122 of the Patent Rules, the requester is notified. Examples of unacceptable requests include those not detailing pertinence/manner of application or based on non-prior-art. A failure to include a required small entity declaration makes the request unacceptable, but the declaration may be submitted without resubmitting the entire request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-compliant requests may be corrected and resubmitted without further fee. A request is not considered to have been made until compliant; no action on the merits until acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: First stage — substantial new question (SNQ) threshold and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Within three months of establishment, the re-examination board must determine whether a substantial new question of patentability affecting any claim of the patent is raised by the request (subsection 48.2(2)). To raise a SNQ the request must present an issue relating to validity not previously considered during prosecution or other prior proceedings, and not so closely related to a previously considered issue as to be not 'substantial' and 'new'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SNQ often raised by prior art not on original record; the same prior art can raise a SNQ if applied differently. Absence of evidence of how an examiner considered prior art means the board will not presume it was considered in the same manner as alleged in the request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notifications and patentee reply at first stage
rubrics_metrics.description: If the board determines no SNQ is raised, the requester is notified with reasons and the decision is final and not subject to appeal. If SNQ is raised, the patentee is notified with the board's reasons and may reply within three months with submissions and propose amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Package containing the request and prior art is sent to patentee if requester is not the patentee. If requester is the patentee, no package is sent. The board's reasons are not limited to the arguments set out by the requester.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second stage procedures, amendment rules, and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The second stage begins upon a patentee reply or expiration of three months from notification. The re-examination proceeds on the SNQ; the patentee may propose any amendment to the patent (including description/drawings). Amended or new claims must be numbered consecutively beginning with the next claim number (section 123). No amendment or new claim shall enlarge the scope of a claim of the patent (subsection 48.3(2)); at minimum any proposed claim must include all features of the broadest independent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exchanges may include oral or written submissions; oral submissions can be in person, teleconference, or videoconference. The second stage must be completed within twelve months (subsection 48.3(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion of re-examination — outcomes and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon completion of the second stage, the re-examination board will issue a certificate of re-examination delivered by registered mail. The certificate may: cancel any claim determined unpatentable; confirm any claim determined patentable; or incorporate any proposed amended or new claim determined patentable. Accompanying the certificate will be a decision letter explaining reasons and a registration certificate indicating the re-examination certificate is registered against the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cancellation removes scope of protection but does not necessarily remove text from dependent claims; amendments incorporated will be noted. A new cover page is generated to indicate re-examination. Board determinations are functionally equivalent to a Commissioner decision under section 40 and are reviewed on a reasonableness standard.
